chapter_summary:
Effective filesystem security is the bedrock of a hardened Linux system. While traditional `chmod` and `chown` commands provide a foundational layer of protection, advanced scenarios demand more granular control. This is where Access Control Lists (ACLs) become indispensable. ACLs allow you to define permissions for specific users or groups on a file or directory, overriding or augmenting the standard owner, group, and others permissions. For instance, you might have a directory where the owner has full control, a specific group has read access, but an individual user *not* in that group also needs write access. Without ACLs, this would necessitate creating a new group and adjusting primary group memberships, which can quickly become unwieldy. To manage ACLs, you'll primarily use the `setfacl` and `getfacl` commands. `setfacl -m u:username:rwx /path/to/directory` grants read, write, and execute permissions to `username` on the specified directory. It's crucial to understand the mask entry that ACLs introduce, which defines the maximum permissions that can be granted to any entry other than the owner. If the mask is `r-x`, even if you set `u:user:rwx`, the user will only effectively get `r-x`. Always check the effective permissions with `getfacl`.

Beyond user and group permissions, Linux filesystems offer special attributes that provide an additional layer of security. The `chattr` command, short for "change attributes," allows you to set flags on files and directories that even the root user cannot easily bypass. One of the most powerful attributes for security is the immutable flag, `+i`. When applied to a file (`chattr +i /path/to/file`), that file cannot be modified, deleted, renamed, or linked, even by root, until the `+i` attribute is removed (`chattr -i /path/to/file`). This is incredibly useful for critical system configuration files like `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, or `/etc/fstab`, preventing accidental or malicious alteration. Another useful attribute is `+a`, the append-only flag, which allows data to be added to a file but not overwritten or deleted, ideal for sensitive log files. However, use these attributes judiciously; locking down too many files can hinder legitimate system operations or troubleshooting. A common mistake is applying `+i` to a log file, which prevents log rotation from working correctly, leading to disk space issues. Always test the impact of `chattr` attributes in a controlled environment before deploying them in production.

Securing filesystems also involves configuring appropriate mount options in `/etc/fstab`. When mounting partitions, especially those containing user data or temporary files, certain options can significantly enhance security. For instance, the `noexec` option prevents the execution of binaries on that filesystem, effectively mitigating risks from malicious scripts or executables placed in user home directories or `/tmp`. The `nosuid` option prevents set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits from taking effect, which can prevent privilege escalation attacks. The `nodev` option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the filesystem, which is useful for preventing device files from being created or exploited in non-system partitions. For `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`, using a `tmpfs` mount with `noexec,nosuid,nodev` is a highly recommended practice, as it stores these temporary files in RAM, improving security and performance by ensuring they are cleared on reboot. Regularly auditing your `/etc/fstab` for these hardening options is a critical security practice.

Finally, a robust security posture requires continuous auditing. Periodically reviewing filesystem permissions and attributes helps identify drift from your security baseline. Tools like `find` can be invaluable for this. For example, `find / -perm /4000` will locate all files with the SUID bit set, which are potential privilege escalation vectors that need careful review. Similarly, `find / -type f -exec getfacl {} +` can help you audit ACLs across your system. For critical directories, you might want to establish a baseline of permissions and use a file integrity monitoring tool (which we'll discuss later) to detect unauthorized changes. Remember that permissions are dynamic; new applications, user changes, and system updates can all alter them. Establishing a regular schedule for these audits, perhaps as part of a weekly or monthly security checklist, is essential for maintaining a secure environment. Always perform these audits with appropriate logging and consider using configuration management tools like Ansible to enforce desired states, reducing the manual effort and potential for human error.

screens.title: Securing Filesystems and Permissions
screens.subtitle: Advanced ACLs, file attributes, secure mounts, and auditing for a hardened Linux host

narration.text: Effective filesystem security protects your system at the most fundamental level. In this lesson you will learn how ACLs give you per-user and per-group control beyond the classic owner-group-others model, how file attributes like immutable and append-only add a layer of protection that even root must respect until the attribute is removed, and how mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev mitigate common attack paths. We will also cover practical auditing commands you can run to find misconfigurations, and a hands-on scenario that ties ACLs and chattr together for a critical application directory and an important log file. This matters because permissions drift and misapplied attributes are common causes of vulnerabilities in production systems. You will see concrete examples using setfacl, getfacl, chattr, and find, and you will learn common pitfalls to avoid — for example, how an immutable flag can break log rotation if applied to the wrong file. By the end, you’ll be able to reason about when ACLs are appropriate, when to apply special attributes, and how to enforce and audit these settings on a schedule.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Filesystem permissions, ACLs, file attributes, and secure mount options form a layered defense. Together they reduce the attack surface and limit how an adversary or misconfigured process can modify critical files.

First, you will be able to use Access Control Lists to grant specific users or groups precise access without changing file ownership. Second, you will learn to apply and remove special file attributes like immutable and append-only, and to reason about when these attributes help or harm normal operations. Third, you will master secure mount options in /etc/fstab, knowing how noexec, nosuid, and nodev reduce attack surfaces for non-system volumes and temporary directories. screens.title: What are Access Control Lists (ACLs)?
screens.subtitle: Defining per-user and per-group permissions beyond owner/group/others

narration.text: Access Control Lists extend the traditional UNIX permission model by recording explicit entries for users and groups on a file system object. Where owner, group, and others provide only three buckets of access, ACLs let you say, for example, that a particular developer has write access to a configuration directory even though they are not in the owning group. This reduces the need to change primary group assignments or create temporary groups. Concretely, the setfacl command writes these ACL entries and getfacl displays them. A typical command to grant a user named appuser full access looks like setfacl dash m u:appuser:rwx on the target directory. One important concept that often surprises administrators is the ACL mask — it caps the maximum permissions that any named user or group entry can have. If the mask is set to r-x, then even a user ACL entry set to rwx will effectively be r-x. A common misconception is that setfacl always grants higher access; in fact the mask can silently reduce effective permissions, so always verify with getfacl. In practice, use ACLs for carefully targeted needs and prefer group-based permissions for broad access patterns. To check your work, use getfacl and attempt the intended operations as the target user.

keyIdea.title: ACL definition
keyIdea.text: ACLs provide per-user and per-group permission entries that augment the standard owner-group-others model; always check the mask for effective permissions.

content.html:
Core Concept

What are ACLs?

ACLs let you set permissions for specific users or groups beyond owner, group, and others.

Definition
An ACL is a list of permission entries attached to a file or directory that names users or groups and their permissions.
Common misconception
ACLs always increase access. In reality, the mask can reduce effective permissions, so verification is required.
Key takeaway
Use ACLs for specific exceptions. Maintain group-based control for broader membership rules.
Illustration & Example
Scenario
A shared config directory must allow appadmin full control, appdevs group read access, and a single testuser temporary write access without changing group membership.
Command example
# Grant user write access with ACL
sudo setfacl -m u:testuser:rwx /opt/app/config
# View ACLs
getfacl /opt/app/config
Check your understanding
  • After setfacl, run getfacl to inspect the mask and effective permissions.
  • If a user still cannot write, verify the mask is not restricting access.

narration.text: Working with ACLs is a small workflow: modify ACL entries with setfacl, inspect with getfacl, and verify effective permissions by testing as the target account. Start by adding a user entry: setfacl dash m u:username:rwx on the target path grants read, write, and execute to that user. To avoid surprises, run getfacl afterwards; it shows entries for owner, group, mask, and any named users or groups. Remember that the mask controls the maximum permissions for named entries and group entries. If you set u:alice:rwx but the mask is r-x, alice effectively has only r-x. If you need a group-level exception, add a g: group entry. For directories you may also set default ACLs so newly created files inherit entries: setfacl -d -m u:username:rwx /path. A common mistake is forgetting to add the execute bit on directories when granting write access; without execute permission a user cannot traverse or create files even if they have write on the directory entry. After making changes, always validate by switching user context or using sudo -u to attempt the intended action. This workflow ensures ACLs behave as you expect and avoids latent permission issues that appear in production.

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Modify with setfacl, inspect with getfacl, set defaults for directories, and always validate by testing the operation as the target user.

content.html:
Process Flow

setfacl → getfacl → validate

A simple, repeatable sequence prevents permission surprises in production.

Add a user ACL
sudo setfacl -m u:appadmin:rwx /opt/app/config
# Verify
getfacl /opt/app/config
Default ACL for directories
sudo setfacl -d -m u:appdevs:r-x /opt/app/config
# New files inherit this ACL
getfacl /opt/app/config
Common pitfall
Granting write without execute on a directory blocks traversal. Remember to include execute for directories when adding write privileges.
Verification steps
  1. Run getfacl to confirm entries and observe the mask value.
  2. Use sudo -u username to perform the intended file operation and verify success or failure.
  3. If access is denied, re-check the mask and directory execute bits.
Key Takeaway

Follow a three-step workflow: setfacl to change, getfacl to inspect the mask and entries, and validate by testing as the target user to ensure effective permissions match intent.

screens.title: File Attributes with chattr
screens.subtitle: Immutable and append-only flags for defense-in-depth

narration.text: File attributes on Linux provide behavioral controls that sit above standard permissions. The chattr command modifies these attributes and lsattr or lsattr-equivalent commands display them. Two attributes are especially useful for security: immutable and append-only. The immutable attribute prevents modification, deletion, renaming, and linking of a file until the attribute is removed. This can be invaluable for protecting critical configuration files from accidental or malicious edits. The append-only attribute allows data to be added to a file but prevents overwriting or removal of existing content, which is practical for audit logs. Use chattr plus i to add immutable and plus a for append-only. A common operational pitfall is applying immutable to a file that must be rotated or updated; for example, making a log file immutable will prevent rotation and eventually exhaust disk space. Therefore, apply attributes only after validating that processes that need to write will still function, and document attribute usage so future administrators understand why a file cannot be modified. When you apply attributes, run a quick test cycle: try an expected write and a blocked destructive operation, then remove the attribute and repeat to ensure reversibility.

keyIdea.title: chattr summary
keyIdea.text: chattr sets robust file behavior flags; use +i to make files immutable and +a to allow append-only writes, but test impacts on rotation and services before applying.

content.html:
Definition

chattr: special file attributes

Attributes like immutable (+i) and append-only (+a) add an additional protection layer that operates independently of UNIX permissions.

Immutable (+i)
Prevents modification, deletion, renaming, and linking until removed; useful for critical config files.
Append-only (+a)
Allows only appending data; ideal for preserving log integrity while still recording new entries.
Pitfall
Applying +i to a rotating log prevents rotation and can cause a disk-full condition. Always test in staging first.
Commands & Example
# Make a config file immutable
sudo chattr +i /etc/myapp/config.yml
# Make a log file append-only
sudo chattr +a /var/log/app/critical.log
# Verify attributes
lsattr /var/log/app/critical.log
Pro Tip

Document any use of immutable or append-only attributes and include attribute changes in your change control system so others know why a file is locked.

screens.title: Immutable vs Append-Only
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right attribute for the use case

narration.text: Immutable and append-only attributes are both defensive, but they solve different problems. Immutable prevents any change at all — no writes, no renames, no deletion — making it suitable for static configuration files that must not change between controlled updates. Append-only allows writes, but only to add data at the end of a file; existing content is preserved. This makes append-only ideal for audit logs or append-only ledgers where you need to ensure historical data cannot be overwritten. A common misunderstanding is treating append-only as sufficient for protecting config files; append-only still permits new data to be appended which might not prevent some attack patterns. Conversely, immutable is too rigid for actively written logs or files updated by services. Operational impact is key: immutable can block package updates or service writes; append-only can interfere with rotate-and-truncate approaches. To choose correctly, ask whether the file must accept new data daily or remain unchanged until a managed update window. If unchanged, immutable; if only appending is required, append-only. Always test removal and reapplication procedures so maintenance tasks remain possible. Immutable vs Append-Only means use immutable for static, rarely changed configuration; use append-only for logs and audit trails that require additive writes only.. In practical terms, choosing the right attribute for the use case. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Attribute selection
keyIdea.text: Use immutable for static, rarely changed configuration; use append-only for logs and audit trails that require additive writes only.

content.html:
Comparison
Immutable (+i)
  • Prevents all modification and deletion
  • Good for critical configs
  • Can prevent updates and rotations
Append-only (+a)
  • Allows only appending
  • Ideal for logs and audit files
  • Can interfere with truncation-based rotation
Misconception check
Neither attribute substitutes for correct ACLs and ownership. They are complementary and should be used where their operational constraints are understood and acceptable.
Concrete example
Protecting /etc/passwd
Applying immutable to a critical system file prevents accidental or adversarial edits. But you must remove it during controlled updates.
Protecting audit logs
Append-only on a log file ensures entries cannot be erased while still allowing new records to be written.
Key Takeaway

Choose attributes based on intended file lifecycle: immutable for static files, append-only for append-only streams, and always test operational impact before deployment.

screens.title: Secure Mount Options in /etc/fstab
screens.subtitle: Applying noexec, nosuid, and nodev to reduce attack surface

narration.text: Mount options are an important line of defense for entire filesystems. When a partition is mounted with noexec, it prevents direct execution of binaries from that filesystem. nosuid disables the set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits, stopping unexpected privilege elevation through executable SUID files on that mount. nodev prevents character or block device files from being interpreted, which reduces the risk of device-based exploits. These options are particularly useful for user data partitions and temporary directories where executing arbitrary binaries or creating device files must be blocked. A practical example is mounting /tmp or a user home partition with noexec,nosuid,nodev or using tmpfs for /tmp with those options. Remember that noexec is not a complete sandbox — scripts invoked by interpreters may still run if the interpreter is executed from an allowed path and reads the script, so treat noexec as a mitigation rather than a full containment mechanism. Always test applications for compatibility after changing mount options, as some legitimate software may rely on execution or SUID behavior on certain mounts. Secure Mount Options in /etc/fstab means use noexec, nosuid, and nodev for non-system mounts to block common exploitation paths, and test compatibility before deployment.. In practical terms, applying noexec, nosuid, and nodev to reduce attack surface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mount hardening
keyIdea.text: Use noexec, nosuid, and nodev for non-system mounts to block common exploitation paths, and test compatibility before deployment.

content.html:
Core Concept

Secure Mount Options

Apply mount options to reduce risky operations on non-system filesystems.

noexec
Prevents execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem.
nosuid
Disables SUID and SGID bits from taking effect on this mount.
nodev
Blocks interpretation of device files on the filesystem.
Example /etc/fstab entry
# Mount /tmp as tmpfs with hardening options
tmpfs /tmp tmpfs defaults,noexec,nosuid,nodev 0 0
# A data partition with nodev and noexec
/dev/sdb1 /mnt/data ext4 defaults,nodev,noexec 0 2
Misconception check

noexec stops direct binary execution but does not block interpreters from loading scripts; treat it as part of a layered defense rather than a complete control.

screens.title: Using tmpfs for /tmp and /var/tmp
screens.subtitle: Why tmpfs plus noexec,nosuid,nodev is recommended for temporary directories

narration.text: A recommended practice for temporary directories is to mount them as tmpfs with the noexec,nosuid,nodev options. tmpfs stores contents in R A M rather than on block storage, so files are cleared automatically on reboot which reduces persistence of malicious files. Combining tmpfs with noexec prevents execution from /tmp, nosuid stops privilege escalation through setuid binaries placed there, and nodev prevents device node creation. This increases security and can improve performance for heavy temporary file usage. When implementing, add an /etc/fstab entry such as tmpfs /tmp tmpfs defaults,noexec,nosuid,nodev 0 0. Always confirm that applications which legitimately execute temporary helpers are not broken by this change, because some installers or applications expect to execute binaries from /tmp. If an application requires execution, consider creating a controlled location with tighter ACLs or adjust only that application's behavior. After adding the mount, test typical workflows, check that the mount options take effect with mount or findmnt, and monitor for unexpected failures. The goal is to reduce attack surface while maintaining application functionality. Using tmpfs for /tmp and /var/tmp means mount /tmp and /var/tmp as tmpfs with noexec,nosuid,nodev to limit persistence and execution of untrusted files while improving security and often performance.. In practical terms, why tmpfs plus noexec,nosuid,nodev is recommended for temporary directories. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: tmpfs benefits
keyIdea.text: Mount /tmp and /var/tmp as tmpfs with noexec,nosuid,nodev to limit persistence and execution of untrusted files while improving security and often performance.

content.html:
Process Flow

Implement tmpfs for temporary dirs

tmpfs keeps temporary files in RAM and clears them on reboot. Use with mount hardening options for extra protection.

Add to /etc/fstab
tmpfs /tmp tmpfs defaults,noexec,nosuid,nodev 0 0
Validation
  • Run mount or findmnt to confirm options.
  • Test common application workflows to detect compatibility issues.
  • If execution is required, create a controlled exception with strict ACLs.
Why it matters
Without tmpfs and hardened options, an attacker can drop a binary into /tmp and execute it, or create device files. This practice reduces these vectors and makes temporary files ephemeral.
Key Takeaway

Use tmpfs plus noexec,nosuid,nodev for /tmp and /var/tmp to reduce execution and device-related risks and to avoid persistent malicious files across reboots.

screens.title: Auditing Permissions with find and getfacl
screens.subtitle: Search for risky SUID/SGID files and collect ACL traces

narration.text: Regular auditing helps you discover configuration drift and potential privilege escalation vectors. One important audit is locating files with the SUID bit set, which can be abused to gain elevated privileges. Use find slash hyphenperm slash 4000 to locate files with SUID; the leading slash indicates a system-wide search. Similarly, run find slash hyphenperm slash 2000 to find SGID files. Once you identify candidates, inspect their ACLs with getfacl to see named user or group entries and confirm whether the mask restricts or allows unexpected access. For broader ACL auditing, you can run find slash type f -exec getfacl {} plus to collect ACLs for many files and then parse the output for anomalies. Establish a baseline snapshot of SUID, SGID, and ACL outputs and compare them on a schedule to detect unauthorized changes. A common mistake is ignoring ACLs during audits; a file might have restrictive traditional permissions but an ACL entry may grant access to a user unexpectedly. Automate these checks if possible and store logs of audits for review and incident response. Auditing Permissions with find and getfacl means use find to locate suid/sgid files and getfacl to inspect acls; establish baselines and schedule regular checks to detect drift.. In practical terms, search for risky suid/sgid files and collect acl traces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Audit commands
keyIdea.text: Use find to locate SUID/SGID files and getfacl to inspect ACLs; establish baselines and schedule regular checks to detect drift.

content.html:
Process Flow

Audit: find SUID/SGID and inspect ACLs

# Find SUID files
find / -perm /4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
# Find SGID files
find / -perm /2000 -type f 2>/dev/null
# Collect ACLs for critical directories
find /etc /opt/app -type f -exec getfacl {} + 2>/dev/null
Best practices
  • Record a baseline of SUID/SGID and ACL outputs for comparison.
  • Schedule weekly or monthly audits depending on change rate.
  • Investigate any newly discovered SUID files immediately; assess their need and provenance.
Common mistake

Only scanning traditional permissions misses ACL entries that grant unexpected access. Include getfacl outputs in your audits.

screens.title: Hands-on: Secure /opt/app/config and a log file
screens.subtitle: Apply ACLs, attributes, and validate the setup

narration.text: Let's walk through the provided hands-on scenario step by step. First, create the group and users, then set ownership and baseline permissions on the configuration directory. The goal is appadmin full control, the appdevs group read access, and no access for others. Next, add ACL entries with setfacl to make the intent explicit. Then create the log file, set ownership and permissions, and apply both append-only and immutable attributes to ensure historical entries are preserved and the file cannot be removed. After each step, verify with getfacl and lsattr or ls -l to confirm effective state. Test as each user: try creating a file as appadmin, reading as a testuser, and appending to the log. If a verification fails, re-check the ACL mask and directory execute bits. Finally, demonstrate how to remove attributes when maintenance is needed using chattr -i and chattr -a, and then reapply them after updates. This practical flow reinforces the interplay between ACLs, ownership, and attributes and shows how to validate protection in a predictable way. Hands-on: Secure /opt/app/config and a log file means create users/groups, set ownership and permissions, apply acls, protect logs with chattr, and validate operations from the intended user contexts.. In practical terms, apply acls, attributes, and validate the setup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hands-on flow
keyIdea.text: Create users/groups, set ownership and permissions, apply ACLs, protect logs with chattr, and validate operations from the intended user contexts.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Secure /opt/app/config and /var/log/app/critical.log

Follow these commands in a controlled environment to apply ACLs and attributes as shown in the chapter source.
# Create group and users
sudo groupadd appdevs
sudo useradd -m appadmin
sudo usermod -aG appdevs appadmin
sudo useradd -m testuser

# Set up directory and ownership
sudo mkdir -p /opt/app/config
sudo chown appadmin:appdevs /opt/app/config
sudo chmod 750 /opt/app/config

# Apply ACLs
sudo setfacl -m u:appadmin:rwx /opt/app/config
sudo setfacl -m g:appdevs:r-x /opt/app/config
sudo setfacl -m o::--- /opt/app/config
getfacl /opt/app/config

# Secure the log file
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/app
sudo touch /var/log/app/critical.log
sudo chown appadmin:appdevs /var/log/app/critical.log
sudo chmod 640 /var/log/app/critical.log
sudo chattr +a+i /var/log/app/critical.log
lsattr /var/log/app/critical.log
Tests to run
  • sudo -u appadmin touch /opt/app/config/admin_file.txt should succeed.
  • sudo -u testuser cat /opt/app/config/admin_file.txt should fail.
  • echo "First log" | sudo tee -a /var/log/app/critical.log should append.
  • Trying to overwrite or delete the log should fail until attributes are removed.
Reminder

Run this scenario in a staging environment first and document attribute changes before applying on production systems.

screens.title: Establishing Baselines and Regular Audits
screens.subtitle: How to detect drift and enforce desired permission states

narration.text: Hardening is not a one-time task; permissions drift as users, applications, and updates change the filesystem. Establish a baseline snapshot that records current SUID, SGID files, ACL outputs for critical directories, and important file attributes. Store those outputs in an audit repository and run scheduled comparisons to identify unexpected changes. When an anomaly appears, investigate whether it was a planned change or a potential compromise. Automating enforcement reduces manual effort: configuration management can enforce ownership, modes, and even run setfacl to maintain ACLs. The chapter recommends using a file integrity monitoring tool later to detect modifications; in the meantime, commands like find and getfacl combined with versioned baseline files are practical. A common error is only auditing once; build a cadence — weekly scans for SUID/SGID files and monthly complete ACL audits are reasonable starting points depending on change frequency. Log audit results, retain them for investigation, and integrate findings into your incident response process. The key is repeatability: a documented audit procedure and baseline lets you detect drift before it becomes a security incident. Best Practice

Baselines and scheduled audits

Record the outputs of your permission and attribute scans, store them versioned, and compare regularly to detect drift.

Baseline commands
find / -perm /4000 -type f > baseline_suid.txt
find / -type f -exec getfacl {} + > baseline_acls.txt
lsattr -R /etc > baseline_attrs.txt
Audit cadence
  • Weekly: SUID/SGID scan and quick ACL diff for high-change dirs.
  • Monthly: Full ACL collection and attribute inventory.
  • On change: Run targeted audits after major deployments or user provisioning.
Automation & Enforcement
Use configuration management to enforce ownership, modes, and ACLs where appropriate. Automation reduces human error and keeps your baseline intact.
Key Takeaway

Audits must be repeatable, scheduled, and tied to incident response. Make baselines and automate enforcement to prevent drift and detect unauthorized changes quickly.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Misconceptions
screens.subtitle: What tripped up admins and how to avoid it

narration.text: Experienced administrators sometimes fall into predictable mistakes when hardening filesystems. One frequent error is thinking that noexec alone stops all forms of code execution; it blocks direct execution, but interpreters can still read and execute scripts if invoked from elsewhere. Another common mistake is applying immutable indiscriminately — for instance, making a log file immutable prevents rotation and can cause disk exhaustion. A related misconception is relying solely on filesystem attributes as a security control without auditing ACLs; a file might be owned correctly yet have ACL entries that grant broader access. Some teams overuse ACLs and create complex permission sets that are hard to audit and maintain; prefer group-based access for broad needs and reserve ACLs for exceptions. Also, failing to check the ACL mask leads to surprising denials. To avoid these pitfalls, test changes in staging, document exceptions, record baselines, and include ACL outputs in audits. When in doubt, adopt the least privilege principle: grant only the access needed and remove attributes or ACL entries when they are no longer necessary. Advanced Guidance

Common mistakes

  • Relying on noexec as a single control; it is a mitigation, not a sandbox.
  • Applying immutable to files that must be rotated or updated.
  • Overcomplicated ACLs that are hard to audit and maintain.
  • Ignoring the ACL mask when debugging access issues.
Remediation steps
Test in staging and validate application behavior after mount or attribute changes.
Document and include attribute changes in change control to avoid surprises.
Prefer group-based controls for broad access; use ACLs for targeted exceptions only.
Include ACL outputs in your scheduled audits and baseline records.
Key Takeaway

Avoid shortcuts. Combine mount hardening, ACLs, file attributes, and regular audits to create a resilient, maintainable security posture.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Remember three pillars when securing filesystems: precise permissions with ACLs, protective file attributes, and hardened mount options. ACLs let you grant user-specific or group-specific access without changing ownership, but always check the mask and validate by testing as the target user. chattr attributes such as immutable and append-only provide an extra defense layer, but they have operational consequences — immutable can block updates and append-only can break certain rotation strategies. Mount options like noexec, nosuid, and nodev limit risky behaviors on non-system filesystems and are especially valuable when applied to tmpfs mounts for /tmp and /var/tmp. Finally, auditing is not optional: use find to locate SUID/SGID files and getfacl to collect ACLs, establish baselines, and run scheduled comparisons. These measures together reduce the attack surface, help prevent privilege escalation, and make it easier to detect unauthorized changes. Keep your procedures repeatable and documented so these protections remain effective over time.

keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: ACLs, file attributes, and mount hardening, combined with regular audits, form a layered defense for filesystem security.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.1 › Key Concepts
Access Control Lists (ACLs)
Define per-user or per-group permissions beyond owner/group/others for targeted access control.
File Attributes (chattr)
Immutable (+i) and append-only (+a) protect files at a behavioral level; test impacts on system processes.
Mount Options & tmpfs
Use noexec,nosuid,nodev and tmpfs for temporary directories to limit execution, privilege escalation, and device creation.
Summary

Combine ACLs, attributes, and mount hardening with scheduled audits to maintain a secure filesystem baseline and detect drift early.

narration.text: As you apply these controls in real environments, keep a few practical rules: prefer group-based permissions for regular membership changes and use ACLs for exceptions; always inspect the ACL mask when access behaves unexpectedly; test chattr attributes in staging to avoid breaking rotations or updates; and automate permission audits and baselines to catch drift. When adding mount hardening, validate application compatibility because noexec and nosuid can break expected behaviors. Finally, document every exception and keep an audit trail of attribute and ACL changes. These habits make filesystem hardening sustainable and reduce surprises during maintenance or investigation. If you treat permissions as a living part of your operational hygiene, you'll prevent many common security incidents and make root cause analysis faster when something does go wrong.
